why: Publishing to an SNS topic that fans out to multiple SQS queues decouples the producer from dozens of consumers. Each consumer reads from its own queue at its own pace, and SNS plus SQS standard queues scale virtually without limit, absorbing sudden spikes to 100,000 messages per second.

others.A: Kinesis Data Analytics is for running SQL/Flink analytics on streams, not a message store that dozens of consumers read from.
others.B: Scaling the ingestion tier on CPU does not decouple producers from consumers and reacts too slowly to sudden spikes.
others.C: A single Kinesis shard is limited to 1,000 records per second for writes, far below 100,000 messages per second, and DynamoDB polling adds coupling.

tip: Many consumers plus decoupling plus bursty volume = SNS fan-out to SQS queues.

why: AWS Secrets Manager supports multi-Region secret replication, keeping replica secrets in sync across Regions, and has built-in scheduled rotation for Amazon RDS for MySQL. This fully managed approach rotates credentials across Regions with the least operational overhead.

others.B: Systems Manager Parameter Store secure strings do not offer built-in multi-Region replication or native scheduled rotation.
others.C: Storing credentials in S3 and rotating them with custom Lambda code is a do-it-yourself solution with much more overhead.
others.D: A DynamoDB global table plus KMS keys plus custom Lambda and RDS API calls reinvents what Secrets Manager provides natively.

tip: Rotating database credentials, especially across Regions = Secrets Manager with rotation and replication.

why: AWS Network Firewall is a managed, stateful network firewall and intrusion prevention service for VPCs. It inspects and filters traffic flowing in and out of the production VPC, replicating the on-premises inspection server's traffic flow inspection and filtering functions.

others.A: GuardDuty is a threat detection service that analyzes logs; it does not inline-inspect or filter traffic.
others.B: Traffic Mirroring copies traffic for out-of-band analysis but cannot filter or block it.
others.D: Firewall Manager centrally manages firewall policies across accounts; it is not itself the inspection engine.

tip: Inline VPC traffic inspection and filtering = AWS Network Firewall.

why: Gateway Load Balancer is built to deploy, scale and manage third-party virtual appliances such as firewalls, passing IP packets transparently using GENEVE. A Gateway Load Balancer endpoint in the application VPC receives incoming traffic and sends it to the GWLB and appliance in the inspection VPC before it reaches the web servers.

others.A: A Network Load Balancer forwards to targets at layer 4 but is not designed for transparent bump-in-the-wire appliance insertion.
others.B: An Application Load Balancer terminates HTTP(S) connections and cannot pass raw IP packets to an appliance for inspection.
others.C: A transit gateway routes between VPCs but does not by itself insert, load balance or scale an inspection appliance with low overhead.

tip: Third-party firewall/IDS appliances inline = Gateway Load Balancer plus GWLB endpoints.

why: The keyed answer C uses NLBs (which support UDP) behind a Route 53 latency record. However, it places Amazon CloudFront in front, and CloudFront only handles HTTP/HTTPS, so it cannot carry VoIP UDP traffic. NLBs as AWS Global Accelerator endpoints (option A) route UDP users to the lowest-latency Region over the AWS backbone with automatic health-based failover.

others.A: This is actually the best design: Global Accelerator supports UDP, routes to the nearest healthy Region, and fails over automatically.
others.B: ALBs do not support UDP, so they cannot serve the VoIP traffic even behind Global Accelerator.
others.D: ALBs do not support UDP, CloudFront does not carry UDP, and weighted routing does not pick the lowest-latency Region.

tip: UDP plus multi-Region lowest latency plus fast failover = Global Accelerator with NLB endpoints.
flag: The keyed answer C is likely wrong: CloudFront cannot carry UDP. A (NLBs as AWS Global Accelerator endpoints) is the accepted answer.

why: Kinesis Data Streams ingests millions of transactions in near real time and lets several internal applications consume the same stream concurrently. A Lambda consumer removes sensitive data from each record and writes the sanitized transactions to DynamoDB, a document database with low-latency retrieval.

others.A: DynamoDB has no built-in rule to strip sensitive data on write, and raw data would be stored before any sanitization.
others.B: Kinesis Data Firehose cannot deliver to DynamoDB, and consuming from S3 is not near real time for other applications.
others.D: Batched files in S3 are not near real time, and reprocessing files adds latency.

tip: Near-real-time sharing with multiple consumers = Kinesis Data Streams; Firehose is for delivery to stores like S3/Redshift/OpenSearch.

why: Provisioned IOPS SSD (io1/io2) storage delivers consistent, high I/O performance with low latency, suited to I/O-intensive workloads with millions of daily writes. Because storage performance is the bottleneck, moving from General Purpose SSD to Provisioned IOPS directly addresses the slow inserts.

others.B: A memory optimized instance class helps memory-bound workloads, not a storage I/O bottleneck.
others.C: Burstable instances relate to CPU credits and would not fix storage performance; they could make things worse.
others.D: Read replicas offload reads, but the problem is slow inserts, which still go to the primary.

tip: Storage I/O is the bottleneck for an RDS database = Provisioned IOPS SSD.

why: The certificate must come from an external CA, so it has to be imported into ACM and applied to the ALB. ACM does not auto-renew imported certificates, but it emits expiration events, so an EventBridge rule can notify the team to rotate the certificate manually each year.

others.A: A certificate issued by ACM comes from Amazon's CA, not the required external CA.
others.B: ACM-issued certificates come from Amazon's CA, and you cannot export or import their key material this way.
others.C: ACM Private CA issues private certificates that public browsers do not trust, and it is not the required external CA.

tip: External-CA certificate = import into ACM; imported certificates need manual renewal, so alert on expiry.

why: Storing the .pdf files in S3 and using an S3 PUT event notification to invoke a Lambda function that converts each file and writes the .jpg back to S3 is fully serverless. S3 scales storage automatically and Lambda scales with demand and charges only per use, making this the most cost-effective scalable design.

others.B: DynamoDB items are limited to 400 KB, so 5 MB files cannot be stored there, and it is costly for blob storage.
others.C: EC2 instances and EBS storage must be provisioned and managed, which costs more, and EBS is not shared across instances.
others.D: EC2 fleets cost more than serverless processing, and the option inconsistently stores files in EBS.

tip: Event-driven file processing at scale = S3 event notification plus Lambda.

why: An Application Load Balancer is built for HTTP applications, and its HTTP health checks against the application URL detect HTTP errors. With the Auto Scaling group using ELB health checks, unhealthy instances are replaced automatically, without custom scripts or code.

others.A: The NLB in this scenario is not detecting the application's HTTP errors, and health checks alone do not replace instances.
others.B: A cron job that parses logs and restarts the app is a custom script, which the requirement forbids.
others.D: The NLB's UnhealthyHostCount does not reflect the HTTP errors it fails to detect, and the alarm cannot identify which instances to replace.

tip: Replace instances on application-level errors = ALB HTTP health checks plus ELB health checks in the Auto Scaling group.

why: DynamoDB point-in-time recovery continuously backs up the table and can restore to any second within the last 35 days. That easily meets a 15-minute RPO after data corruption, and restoring to a new table typically completes within the 1-hour RTO.

others.A: Global tables replicate corruption to every Region almost immediately, so they do not protect against bad data.
others.C: Daily exports give an RPO of up to 24 hours, and Glacier retrieval plus import would exceed the 1-hour RTO.
others.D: DynamoDB is a managed service that does not use EBS volumes, so EBS snapshots cannot back it up.

tip: Protection from data corruption in DynamoDB with minutes of RPO = point-in-time recovery.

why: A VPC gateway endpoint for S3 keeps traffic between the EC2 application tier and the bucket on the AWS network. A bucket policy that only allows access from the application tier (for example via aws:SourceVpce or the application's IAM role) ensures nothing else can read the sensitive data.

others.B: Making the objects public exposes sensitive data to everyone.
others.D: Copying long-term IAM user credentials onto instances is insecure; use an instance role instead.
others.E: A NAT instance sends traffic over the internet path and adds management overhead without restricting bucket access.

tip: Private S3 access from a VPC = gateway endpoint plus a bucket policy scoped to that endpoint or role.

why: S3 event notifications to SQS durably capture each upload, and a Lambda function processes queue messages as soon as they arrive, scaling with demand and down to zero. Storing the resulting JSON in DynamoDB keeps everything fully managed, giving the least operational overhead.

others.A: An EMR cluster is heavy to operate for small one-time transformations and does not react immediately to each upload.
others.B: EC2 instances must be provisioned, patched and scaled, which adds overhead for spiky or idle demand.
others.D: Kinesis Data Streams needs shard management and Aurora needs a provisioned cluster, adding overhead over SQS and DynamoDB.

tip: Event-driven, variable volume, least overhead = S3 events to SQS to Lambda.

why: The first statement allows ec2:TerminateInstances when the caller's source IP is in 10.100.100.0/24. The second statement explicitly denies all EC2 actions outside us-east-1. A user whose source IP is 10.100.100.254 is inside the allowed range, so the user can terminate instances in us-east-1 only.

others.A: The Deny statement blocks all EC2 actions in every Region except us-east-1, the opposite of this option.
others.B: aws:SourceIp refers to the caller's IP address, not the IP address of the instance being terminated.
others.D: 10.100.100.254 falls within 10.100.100.0/24, so the Allow applies and nothing denies the action in us-east-1.

tip: aws:SourceIp is the requester's IP; an explicit Deny always overrides an Allow.

why: Lambda scales automatically with highly variable numbers of concurrent users to process photos. Storing photos in Amazon S3 gives virtually unlimited, durable object storage, and keeping DynamoDB for metadata retains a scalable, low-latency metadata store.

others.A: DynamoDB items are limited to 400 KB, so it is not suitable for storing photos.
others.B: Kinesis Data Firehose is a delivery service for streaming data; it does not process photos or act as a store.
others.D: A fixed three EC2 instances do not scale with demand, and EBS volumes are not shared object storage.

tip: Images and large objects go in S3; keep metadata in DynamoDB.

why: A gateway VPC endpoint for S3, linked to the private subnets' route table, sends S3 traffic over the AWS private network instead of the internet. Moving the instances to private subnets removes internet access they do not need.

others.A: A NAT gateway still sends S3 traffic out to the public S3 endpoint over the internet path.
others.B: Security group rules restrict destinations but do not change the route; traffic still goes through the internet gateway.
others.D: Direct Connect links on-premises networks to AWS; it does not provide a private route from EC2 instances already in a VPC.

tip: EC2 to S3 without the internet = S3 gateway VPC endpoint.

why: With AWS PrivateLink, the provider exposes its service as a VPC endpoint service and the company creates an interface VPC endpoint to it. Traffic stays private, access is limited to that single service, and connections can only be initiated from the company's (consumer) VPC.

others.A: VPC peering opens routing between whole networks rather than just the target service, and either side can initiate traffic.
others.B: A virtual private gateway is for VPN or Direct Connect connectivity and is not how PrivateLink services are exposed.
others.C: A NAT gateway sends traffic over the internet, so the connection would not be private.

tip: Private, service-specific, consumer-initiated access to another VPC's service = AWS PrivateLink.

why: CloudFront accelerates both static and dynamic content: it caches static objects at edge locations and, for dynamic personalized requests, terminates TLS near users and uses persistent connections over the AWS backbone to the ALB origin. That gives the lowest latency for users worldwide from a single-Region stack.

others.B: Two Regions still leave many users far from an origin, and nothing is cached at the edge.
others.C: Serving dynamic content directly from the ALB gives distant users full round trips over the public internet.
others.D: Geolocation routing to two Regions without an edge network still leaves high latency for users far from both Regions.

tip: CloudFront helps dynamic content too, through edge TLS termination and backbone routing.

why: AWS Shield Advanced provides enhanced DDoS detection and mitigation for ALBs, CloudFront, Route 53 and Global Accelerator. It adds 24/7 Shield Response Team support, cost protection and automatic application-layer mitigation through AWS WAF.

others.A: Amazon Inspector scans EC2, containers and Lambda for vulnerabilities; it is not installed on an ALB and does not stop DDoS.
others.B: Amazon Macie discovers sensitive data in S3; it does not prevent attacks.
others.D: GuardDuty detects threats from logs but does not mitigate DDoS attacks.

tip: DDoS protection beyond the default = AWS Shield Advanced.

why: AWS WAF on the ALB supports geographic match rules, so a web ACL can allow requests from the one approved country and block all others. Security groups and network ACLs work only on IP addresses and ports and cannot match by country.

others.A: Security groups cannot filter by country, and instances behind the ALB see the ALB as the source.
others.B: ALB security groups only allow IP ranges and ports, not geographic locations.
others.D: Network ACLs filter by IP and port only and would need an unmanageable list of country IP ranges.

tip: Allow or block by country = AWS WAF geo match (or CloudFront geo restriction).

why: A gateway VPC endpoint for DynamoDB keeps traffic from the private subnets on the AWS network without internet, NAT or public IP access. Endpoint policies can also restrict which tables are reachable, making it the most secure option at no extra charge.

others.B: A NAT gateway sends traffic to DynamoDB's public endpoint over the internet path.
others.C: A NAT instance still routes traffic to the public endpoint and is self-managed; it also cannot work from a private subnet.
others.D: Using the internet gateway sends traffic over the internet and requires public IPs.

tip: Private access to S3 or DynamoDB = gateway VPC endpoint.

why: AWS WAF on API Gateway blocks SQL injection and other web exploits at the API entry point. AWS Shield Advanced on the NLB adds detection and mitigation of large, sophisticated DDoS attacks, plus Shield Response Team support and cost protection.

others.A: AWS WAF cannot be associated with a Network Load Balancer.
others.D: GuardDuty detects threats but does not mitigate attacks, and Shield Standard only covers common infrastructure-layer DDoS.
others.E: Shield Standard is automatic and basic; it does not give advanced detection and mitigation of sophisticated DDoS attacks.

tip: SQL injection = AWS WAF; large sophisticated DDoS = Shield Advanced.

why: AWS Transfer Family provides a fully managed, highly available SFTP endpoint that writes uploaded files directly to an S3 bucket. There are no servers, scripts or load balancers to run, which minimizes operational overhead.

others.B: S3 File Gateway exposes NFS and SMB shares, not SFTP.
others.C: Self-managed EC2 instances, a VPN and cron scripts add a lot of operational overhead.
others.D: An NLB with EC2 SFTP servers and cron scripts works but has far more overhead than a managed service.

tip: Managed SFTP/FTPS/FTP into S3 or EFS = AWS Transfer Family.

why: An SQS queue durably buffers incoming requests so bursts do not exceed DynamoDB's provisioned write throughput. Lambda then drains the queue at a controlled rate, so requests are no longer lost and existing users are not throttled.

others.A: Throttling at API Gateway would reject user requests, which impacts existing users.
others.B: DAX is a read cache; it does not buffer or absorb writes.
others.C: A secondary index adds write cost and does nothing to absorb write bursts.

tip: Protect a throughput-limited backend from bursts = put an SQS queue in front of it.

why: AWS WAF is a managed web application firewall that attaches directly to an ALB. AWS managed rule groups block SQL injection and cross-site scripting with no servers to manage, reducing the company's share of responsibility.

others.B: S3 static hosting cannot run the application backend and does not provide traffic filtering.
others.C: Shield Advanced focuses on DDoS protection; filtering XSS and SQL injection is done by WAF rules.
others.D: A third-party firewall on EC2 adds servers to patch and manage, increasing the company's responsibility.

tip: XSS/SQL injection filtering on ALB, API Gateway or CloudFront = AWS WAF.

why: Transferring 700 TB at 500 Mbps would take about 130 days, far beyond the 1-month deadline, so offline AWS Snowball devices are required. A Lifecycle policy to S3 Glacier Deep Archive gives the cheapest storage for rarely accessed data kept for 7 years.

others.B: A VPN over the same 500 Mbps link is still far too slow for 700 TB in a month.
others.C: A 500 Mbps Direct Connect link has the same bandwidth limit, plus provisioning time and cost.
others.D: DataSync over 500 Mbps cannot move 700 TB in a month, and S3 Glacier costs more than Deep Archive.

tip: Compute transfer time: if the network cannot finish in time, use the Snow Family.

why: Giving the pod an IAM role (IAM roles for service accounts or EKS Pod Identity) provides temporary credentials scoped to that pod. A gateway VPC endpoint for DynamoDB keeps traffic from the private subnets on the AWS network without internet access.

others.B: IAM users cannot be attached to pods; workloads should use roles with temporary credentials.
others.C: Network ACL changes do not create a private path; without an endpoint, traffic would need a NAT or internet route.
others.E: Embedding access keys in code is a security anti-pattern.

tip: AWS access from EKS pods = IAM role for the service account; private service access = VPC endpoint.

why: A VPC peering connection between VPC A and VPC B lets the application reach the database over private IP addresses on the AWS network. Security groups can then allow only the application server, and nothing is exposed publicly.

others.A: Allowing all traffic from a public IP requires the database to be reachable publicly, which is less secure.
others.C: Making the database publicly accessible exposes it to the internet.
others.D: A public proxy instance adds an internet-exposed hop and a single point of failure to manage.

tip: Private connectivity between two VPCs = VPC peering (or Transit Gateway at scale).

why: VPC peering works across AWS accounts and connects the two VPCs over the AWS network using private IP addresses. A peering connection is not a single physical device, so it has no single point of failure or bandwidth bottleneck.

others.B: Gateway endpoints are only for S3 and DynamoDB, not for reaching EC2 instances in another VPC.
others.C: A virtual private gateway terminates VPN or Direct Connect connections, which adds tunnels with bandwidth limits.
others.D: Private VIFs belong to Direct Connect for on-premises connectivity, not VPC-to-VPC access.

tip: Cross-account VPC-to-VPC private access with no single point of failure = VPC peering.

why: An internet-facing ALB must be placed in public subnets, which route to an internet gateway, in each Availability Zone. It can then forward traffic to targets in private subnets, so creating public subnets and associating them with the ALB fixes the problem while the instances stay private.

others.A: A NAT gateway only provides outbound access and cannot accept inbound internet traffic, and an NLB does not fix the subnet placement.
others.B: Moving instances to public subnets exposes them needlessly and does not fix the ALB's subnet placement.
others.C: Routing the private subnets to the internet gateway makes them public, and outbound rules do not help inbound traffic.

tip: Internet-facing load balancers live in public subnets; targets can stay private.

why: A NAT gateway in a public subnet, with the private subnet's default route (0.0.0.0/0) pointing to it, lets the instance make outbound connections to download updates. Unsolicited inbound connections from the internet are still blocked.

others.A: Routing the private subnet to the internet gateway makes it a public subnet and requires public IPs on the instance.
others.C: A NAT device must sit in a public subnet; a NAT instance in the private subnet has no internet route.
others.D: Routing the private subnet directly to the internet gateway bypasses the NAT instance and exposes the subnet.

tip: Outbound-only internet access from a private subnet = NAT gateway in a public subnet.

why: Policy1 allows ec2:*, which includes ec2:TerminateInstances, and nothing denies it, so the engineer can delete EC2 instances. The other actions are either only partly allowed (iam:Get*/List*, logs:Get*/Describe*) or explicitly denied (ds:Delete* in Policy2).

others.A: Only iam:Get* and iam:List* are allowed, so iam:DeleteUser is implicitly denied.
others.B: Policy1 allows ds:*, but Policy2's explicit Deny on ds:Delete* overrides it.
others.D: Only logs:Get* and logs:Describe* are allowed, so deleting logs is implicitly denied.

tip: Evaluate IAM as: explicit Deny wins, then an explicit Allow is required, otherwise implicit deny.

why: VPC peering is the cheapest way to connect two VPCs in the same Region: there is no hourly charge, and data transfer within an Availability Zone over peering is free. Add peering routes in both VPCs' route tables and allow the application's security group in the ElastiCache cluster's security group.

others.B: A Transit VPC needs extra appliances or instances and costs more than a simple peering connection.
others.C: A peering connection has no security group; the inbound rule must be on the ElastiCache cluster's security group.
others.D: A Transit VPC costs more, and the rule must be on the ElastiCache security group, not the Transit VPC.

tip: Connecting two VPCs cheaply = VPC peering; reference the source security group in the target's inbound rule.

why: Placing Amazon ElastiCache in front of RDS caches frequently read score data in memory, offloading reads from the database and cutting latency. It improves user experience with minimal change to the existing architecture.

others.B: RDS Proxy pools connections, which helps connection storms but does not reduce read load or speed up read queries.
others.C: Moving compute to Lambda does not address database read performance and is a large architecture change.
others.D: Migrating to DynamoDB requires major application and data model changes.

tip: Database read latency on hot data = add a cache such as ElastiCache.

why: A CloudFront distribution with the existing ALB as origin serves users from edge locations worldwide without rebuilding the stack in other Regions. Caching based on the Accept-Language header stores a separate cached version for each language.

others.A: Replacing a dynamic site with S3 static hosting does not support the dynamic application.
others.C: An API Gateway cache sits in a single Region, so distant users still see high latency.
others.D: Running NGINX cache servers in each Region recreates infrastructure across Regions and adds overhead.

tip: Global low latency without multi-Region deployment = CloudFront in front of the existing origin.

why: Referencing the ALB's security group as the only allowed inbound source in the EC2 instances' security group permits only traffic from the load balancer. All other sources, inside or outside the private subnet, are blocked.

others.A: Route tables cannot route internet traffic directly to private IPs, and routing does not restrict sources.
others.C: Moving instances to public subnets with Elastic IPs exposes them to the internet.
others.D: Opening the ALB security group to any TCP traffic weakens security and does not restrict the instances.

tip: Allow only the load balancer to reach targets = security group rule that references the ALB's security group.

why: A gateway VPC endpoint for S3 adds a route in the VPC route table so traffic to S3 stays on the AWS network and never crosses the internet. Gateway endpoints for S3 have no additional charge.

others.A: A Route 53 private hosted zone handles DNS names but does not create a private network path to S3.
others.C: A NAT gateway sends S3 traffic to the public endpoint through the internet gateway.
others.D: Site-to-Site VPN connects on-premises networks to a VPC; you cannot create a VPN to an S3 bucket.

tip: EC2 to S3 privately = gateway VPC endpoint.

why: FSx for Lustre on persistent SSD storage delivers sub-millisecond latency and very high aggregate throughput for hundreds of Linux clients. Linking it to an S3 bucket lets it import raw data from S3 and export results back.

others.A: Tiering ALL moves data to the capacity pool, which adds latency, and ONTAP is not built for this level of HPC throughput.
others.C: HDD-based Lustre storage cannot deliver sub-millisecond latency.
others.D: FSx for NetApp ONTAP is a general-purpose NAS and is not suited to 6 GBps HPC throughput across hundreds of instances.

tip: HPC on Linux with S3 integration and sub-millisecond latency = FSx for Lustre on SSD.

why: CloudFront caches and delivers the videos from edge locations close to mobile users, which reduces buffering and scales automatically. Amazon Elastic Transcoder (a managed service) converts the large raw videos into mobile-friendly formats and bitrates with no servers to manage.

others.B: Replicating raw files across Regions does not shrink the large videos or cache them near users.
others.D: Running EC2 fleets in Local Zones for caching adds a lot of operational overhead compared with CloudFront.
others.E: A self-managed EC2 transcoding fleet adds operational overhead compared with a managed transcoding service.

tip: Video playback issues = transcode with a managed service and deliver with CloudFront.

why: A Volume Gateway stored volume keeps the full dataset on premises, so users get immediate, low-latency access to all files, while it asynchronously backs up to AWS as EBS snapshots. It presents iSCSI like the existing device, so changes are minimal, and snapshots can be restored to EBS volumes on EC2 for disaster recovery.

others.A: S3 File Gateway changes the protocol to NFS/SMB, requiring application changes, and a 10 TB cache cannot hold hundreds of TB locally.
others.B: Tape gateway backups give slow restores, and the approach changes the existing backup process significantly.
others.C: Cached volumes keep only 10 TB locally, so data outside the cache is fetched from AWS with added latency.

tip: All data must be local with low latency = Volume Gateway stored volumes; only hot data local = cached volumes.

why: AWS Network Firewall inspects traffic routed through it, and its stateful domain list rule groups allow only specified domain names (matched through TLS SNI or HTTP Host headers) while denying everything else. Routing the private subnet's outbound traffic through the firewall enforces the approved-repository policy.

others.B: AWS WAF protects inbound web requests to ALB, API Gateway or CloudFront; it does not filter outbound traffic from EC2.
others.C: Security groups cannot reference URLs or domain names, only IP ranges, ports and other security groups.
others.D: An ALB handles inbound requests to targets; it cannot act as an outbound internet proxy.

tip: Filter outbound traffic by domain name = AWS Network Firewall domain list rules.

why: The batch runs at a known time (midnight on the first day of each month), so a scheduled scaling action can add capacity just before it starts. This prevents the instant CPU spike from disrupting the application, and another scheduled action can scale back in afterwards.

others.A: CloudFront caches content at the edge but does not add compute for a CPU-heavy batch job.
others.B: Simple scaling reacts only after CPU is already at 100%, and new instances take time to launch.
others.D: ElastiCache caches reads; it does not offload a CPU-bound month-end calculation.

tip: Predictable, time-based load = scheduled scaling.

why: Aurora Replicas share the cluster's storage volume, so replica lag is typically well under 100 ms, and Aurora Auto Scaling adds or removes replicas automatically. Aurora MySQL is compatible with the existing application, keeping code changes minimal and operational overhead low.

others.B: Adding a cache and rewriting stored procedures as Lambda functions requires significant code changes and does not fix replication lag.
others.C: Self-managed MySQL on EC2 increases operational overhead, and bigger instances do not remove the cause of lag.
others.D: Migrating to DynamoDB is a major rewrite, and DynamoDB Streams cannot replace stored procedures.

tip: RDS MySQL replica lag problems = migrate to Aurora MySQL with Aurora Replicas.

why: AWS WAF integrates with the ALB, and web ACLs with SQL injection match rules or AWS managed rule groups inspect requests and block SQL injection attempts before they reach the application.

others.B: ALB listener rules match on paths, headers and similar fields but cannot reliably detect SQL injection payloads.
others.C: Shield Advanced is for DDoS protection; SQL injection filtering comes from WAF rules.
others.D: Amazon Inspector scans for vulnerabilities but does not block requests.

tip: SQL injection or XSS protection = AWS WAF web ACL on ALB, API Gateway or CloudFront.

why: The Amazon SQS Extended Client Library for Java stores large payloads in Amazon S3 and sends a reference through SQS, then transparently retrieves the payload when messages are received. It is a drop-in wrapper around the SQS client, so code changes are minimal.

others.B: EventBridge events are limited to 256 KB, and switching services requires substantial code changes.
others.C: The SQS message size limit is a fixed service maximum that cannot be raised to 50 MB.
others.D: SQS cannot natively reference EFS, so this would need custom code to store and fetch messages.

tip: SQS messages larger than the size limit = SQS Extended Client Library with S3.

why: AWS Global Accelerator supports UDP listeners and brings players onto the AWS global network at the nearest edge location, reducing latency, jitter and packet loss. Endpoint groups in each of the eight Regions provide health-based routing to the closest healthy endpoint.

others.A: Transit gateway peering connects VPC networks but does not improve the path from end users to AWS.
others.C: CloudFront serves HTTP/HTTPS and WebSocket traffic; it cannot carry UDP game traffic.
others.D: VPC peering connects VPCs and has no UDP setting; it does nothing for user-to-AWS latency.

tip: UDP plus global users plus low latency = AWS Global Accelerator.

why: Kinesis Data Streams preserves record order within a shard, and using the payment ID as the partition key sends all records for a payment to the same shard. An SQS FIFO queue with the payment ID as the message group ID guarantees ordered delivery for each payment.

others.A: DynamoDB is a database and does not deliver messages in the order they were sent.
others.C: Memcached is a cache with no ordering or messaging semantics.
others.D: SQS standard queues provide best-effort ordering only, and message attributes do not change that.

tip: Ordering per key = Kinesis partition key or SQS FIFO message group ID.

why: One AWS Direct Connect connection gives consistent, low-latency bandwidth to the data center and lower data transfer out rates than the internet. A transit gateway attached to all three VPCs, and to Direct Connect through a Direct Connect gateway, handles both inter-VPC and on-premises routing cost-effectively.

others.A: VPNs over the internet give inconsistent latency for latency-sensitive traffic and do not connect the VPCs to each other.
others.B: Self-managed appliances and IPsec tunnels over the internet add cost and overhead and give inconsistent latency.
others.C: Three Direct Connect connections cost much more than one shared connection, and they do not provide inter-VPC routing.

tip: Many VPCs plus on-premises with consistent performance = one Direct Connect plus a transit gateway.

why: A TLS listener on the NLB with a server certificate (for example from ACM) encrypts client traffic in transit and terminates TLS at the load balancer. This directly improves the security of the sensor data in transit.

others.B: Shield Advanced and WAF protect against attacks; they do not encrypt data in transit, and WAF cannot be attached to an NLB.
others.C: AWS WAF filters web requests but does not encrypt data in transit.
others.D: EBS encryption protects data at rest, not in transit.

tip: Data in transit = TLS listeners and certificates; data at rest = KMS encryption.

why: The key pairs sticky sessions on the ALB, which keeps a user on the same instance during a transaction, with an ElastiCache for Redis cluster as a shared external session store. Redis supports replication, Multi-AZ failover and persistence, so session state survives an instance failing or being scaled in.

others.B: DynamoDB is also a valid durable session store, and many consider it a better fit, but it is not the keyed answer here.
others.C: Cognito user pools handle authentication, not application transaction session state.
others.E: Systems Manager Application Manager is for operations management, not session storage.

tip: Shared session state off the instances = ElastiCache (Redis) or DynamoDB; sticky sessions alone are not durable.
